description: We’re a multidisciplinary team of students and builders interested in using data, mathematics, software, and science to understand how our planet is changing. We’re exploring Earth-system trends through NASA observations and models—turning complex environmental data into something people can actually investigate, visualize, and understand.
summary:
Case Closed is a web tool that lets a student ask what's changing where they live and get an answer they can defend. It follows the challenge's five steps. The student picks one of 15 Earth science variables, picks a region (any of 1,647 Philippine towns and cities, a province, a region or the whole country), sets a time period, reads the time series and gets a significance test. A map colours all 223 NASA grid squares over the Philippines by direction and rate of change, so "where is it changing" has an answer at a glance.

Most trend tools stop when the line goes up. Climate months resemble their neighbours, so the usual test is overconfident. Case Closed runs the plain Mann-Kendall test next to the Hamed-Rao version that corrects for this. For Metro Manila air temperature, the plain test gives p = 4e-12 and the corrected test gives p = 0.001. The trend of +0.14 °C per decade is still real, and the second number is the one a student can defend.

The tool also says "not yet" when a record is too short, tells a steady trend from a single jump, and caught a 1999 break in the reanalysis rainfall record. It's built for high school and college students in the Philippines.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Case Closed follows the challenge's five steps in one flow.

1. Variable. The student picks a theme (heat, rain and water, land and farming, sun and sky, air) and then one of 15 variables. Each one has a one-sentence definition and a line on why it matters.

2. Region. The student picks any of 1,647 towns and cities, a province, a region, an island group or the whole Philippines, or taps the map. A town uses its own NASA grid square, about 55 km across. A larger area uses the average of its squares, weighted by land area.

3. Time period. The student sets a start and an end year. The tool won't give a significance verdict on fewer than 20 years.

4. Time series. Exhibit A shows every month. Exhibit B removes the seasons and draws the trend line. Exhibit C calls a second NASA source as a witness when one exists, such as GPM satellite rainfall next to MERRA-2 rainfall. The student then makes their own call before seeing the test.

5. Significance. The verdict answers four questions in plain words. Is there a trend? How much? Is it significant? How sure are we?

The home map colours all 223 grid squares that touch Philippine land by direction and rate of change. For air temperature from 1981 to 2025, 198 squares show a significant rise, 1 shows a significant fall and 24 show no significant trend. A "What's changing here?" panel ranks all 15 variables for the chosen place. Two guided demos walk through a full investigation. Metro Manila shows a significant trend, and Tuguegarao shows a trend that needs more years.

HOW IT WORKS

For every monthly series, the backend does the following.

1. It subtracts each calendar month's average to remove the seasons.

2. It measures the rate with Sen's slope, per decade.

3. It runs the plain Mann-Kendall test and the Hamed-Rao modified Mann-Kendall test, which corrects for autocorrelation. The verdict uses the corrected p-value.

4. It fits a least-squares slope with a 95% range that uses the effective sample size.

5. It runs a Pettitt test on yearly averages, so a record that changed in one jump is reported as a jump and not as a steady trend.

6. It estimates the record length needed to detect the trend (Weatherhead et al., 1998) when the trend isn't significant yet.

For Metro Manila air temperature, a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.52 makes 540 months count like 172 independent ones. The plain test reports p = 4e-12 and the corrected test reports p = 0.001. The map also applies a Benjamini-Hochberg correction, because testing 223 squares at once would let a few look significant by luck.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students learn the lessons most trend tools skip. A rising line isn't proof. "Not significant" doesn't mean nothing is happening. A record can change because the instruments changed and not the climate. The tool is free and needs no login, and every case has a link a teacher can share with a class.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Every value says where it came from. MERRA-2 values are labelled model-based, and satellite values are labelled satellite.

- The data can mislead. Our break detector found that MERRA-2 rainfall, evaporation and soil moisture all jump in 1999 across the whole country at once, so those variables are analysed from 2000. Aqua AIRS surface air temperature was tested and set aside, because it shows cooling in 208 of 223 squares while MERRA-2 shows 2024 as the warmest year.

- We never join two sensors into one series, because the join creates a step that a trend test reads as a trend.

- If a live data call fails, the app shows an error and never another place's data.

- The statistics are covered by 59 automated tests and were checked against real NASA data.

TOOLS

The backend uses Python, FastAPI, NumPy, pymannkendall and httpx. The frontend uses TypeScript, React, Vite, Recharts and Leaflet. The data come from NASA Giovanni (GPM IMERG, GLDAS and Aura OMI), NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and CERES) and Sentinel-5P. The site runs on Vercel and deploys through GitHub Actions.

SI tools. Kiro and Claude Code (AI coding agents) wrote the code under the team's direction, and the team checked the results against real NASA data. Claude also helped with planning, interface design, the logo, written copy and the demo slides in Canva.
